newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Islamists confront police over schools.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Islamists confront police over schools.

text.p: Thousands of Islamist protesters gathered in the centre of Ankara on Tuesday to demonstrate against proposed secularist education reforms, witnesses said.
"Break the hands of those who try to lay a finger on the Koran," chanted the crowd of up to 5,000. Many waved Turkish flags.
Dozens of police in full riot gear, some with attack dogs, charged a group of about 1,000 protesters marching toward the prime ministry building chanting "government resign".
One journalist had a trouser leg ripped off him by one of the dogs as they snapped at the retreating demonstrators. Several protesters suffered minor injuries.

About 200 police backed up by a line of armoured cars with water-cannon skirmished with about 1,000 protesters trying to force their way up one of the city's main boulevards towards the parliament building.
"Islam will rule the world," one group chanted.
A group of women demonstrators -- their heads cloaked and separated from the menfolk in line with strict Islamic practice -- backed the demands from the sidelines.
Earlier, police arrested 55 people as they tried to approach military headquarters, state-run Anatolia news agency said.
Turkish police banned traffic from the centre of the capital after convoys of cars carrying Islamist protesters began gathering at two main mosques in Ankara in the early morning.

The Islamists have said they would march on parliament to protest at government attempts to extend secularist school education in a bill that would effectively close religious schools, known as Imam Hatips.
"It is the nation which has created these schools and they won't be shut," said Kemal Halici, a retired imam, or Islamic prayer leader.
"I want my children to go to an Imam Hatip so they can grow up properly as Moslems," said Ahmet Goktas clutching his two sons aged four and five.
The education bill was one of series of measures demanded by the powerful military to clamp down on what it says is a growing threat of Islamic activism fuelled by religious schooling.

The crowd, stopped from advancing on parliament, vented much of their anger on journalists watching events from the steps of the education ministry. Turkey's secularist media has strongly supported the anti-Islamist measures.
"The media has sold out, how much money do you want," the crowd shouted.
Necmettin Erbakan, Turkey's first Islamist prime minister resigned last month under pressure from the army after failing to implement the demands.
